Seeing Fit Like an Alterations Specialist

Before you touch a seam ripper you must be able to look at a client in a garment and say exactly what is wrong, why, and whether it can be fixed. This module teaches you to read fit and ease, run a calm and accurate fitting, and give honest style advice about what an alteration will and will not achieve.

Most alteration customers walk in with a feeling, not a diagnosis: "it is not sitting well", "it is too tight here", "it looks old". Your first job is to turn that feeling into a clear, measurable problem. To do that you need two ideas: **ease** and **drag lines**. With these two ideas you can explain almost every fitting problem you will meet on blouses, gowns, skirts and trousers.
A woman trying on clothes in front of a mirror
Every alteration starts with the client wearing the garment while you look carefully at how it sits.
Ease: the room between the body and the cloth

**Ease** is the difference between the body measurement and the garment measurement at the same place. If a client's bust is 96 cm and the blouse measures 104 cm around the bust, the blouse has 8 cm of ease. Ease comes in two kinds. **Wearing ease** is the minimum room needed to breathe, sit, bend and raise the arms. **Design ease** is extra room the designer added on purpose to create a style, such as a loose boubou or a flowing kaftan.

Sewing references commonly quote wearing ease of roughly 5 to 6.5 cm at the bust, about 2.5 cm at the waist and about 5 to 7.5 cm at the hip for a fitted woven garment. Treat these as starting guides, not laws. Stretch fabrics need less ease, sometimes none. Evening wear that is worn standing for a short time can be closer than an office dress worn for nine hours. Always ask the client how she will wear the garment.

A client who says her kaftan is "too big" may simply be used to fitted clothes. If you take all the design ease out of a kaftan, it stops being a kaftan and the fabric will pull at the hips when she sits. Ask: does she want it to fit more closely, or does she want a different style?
Drag lines: the garment is telling you where the problem is
A **drag line** is a fold or wrinkle that forms because the fabric is being pulled or has too much room. The direction of the line points towards the cause. Learn to read three patterns.

**Pulling lines (tight):** fine wrinkles that stretch across the body, like rays. Horizontal lines across the hips of a skirt mean the hip is too tight. Lines pointing from the bust to the armhole can mean too little room at the bust.

**Bagging folds (loose):** soft, deep folds that hang. Vertical folds at the back waist of a dress mean there is too much width there. A pool of fabric above the waist at the back often means the back is too long for the client.

**Diagonal drag lines:** lines running at an angle usually point to the part of the body that needs more or less length or width, for example lines running from the neck down to the armhole can mean the shoulders are sloping more than the garment allows.

The five signs of a good fit
**Shoulder seams** sit on top of the shoulder and end at the shoulder bone, not down the arm (unless the style is a dropped shoulder).
**Side seams** hang straight down, at right angles to the floor, without swinging forward or back.
**Waistline** of a fitted garment sits at the natural waist, and the hem is level all round when the client stands relaxed.
**No pulling or bagging** at bust, back, hips or seat when she stands, and she can sit and raise her arms without strain.
**Closures lie flat:** zips do not ripple, buttons do not gape between the buttonholes.
Worked example: is this office dress too big or just loose?

For example, Halima, a bank officer in Kaduna, brings a ready-made fitted dress. She says it "hangs like a sack" at the waist but feels fine elsewhere. You measure her and then measure the dress laid flat, doubling the flat width.
Bust: body 96 cm, dress 102 cm. Ease = 102 - 96 = 6 cm. That is within normal wearing ease, so leave the bust alone.
Waist: body 80 cm, dress 98 cm. Ease = 98 - 80 = 18 cm. Far more than the 2.5 cm guide and more than a fitted style needs.
Hip: body 104 cm, dress 110 cm. Ease = 110 - 104 = 6 cm, comfortable for sitting at a desk.

She wants a fitted look but must sit all day, so you agree a waist ease of about 4 cm. Target waist = 80 + 4 = 84 cm, so 98 - 84 = 14 cm must be removed at the waist, tapering to nothing at bust and hip.
The problem is only the waist. You write "remove 14 cm at waist, taper to 0 at bust and hip" on her job card, instead of the vague note "take in dress".
Measure the garment correctly

Lay the garment flat, close the zip or buttons, smooth it without stretching and measure straight across from fold to fold. Double that number to get the full circumference. Measure stretch fabrics relaxed, never pulled.

Some fit problems cannot be solved by an alteration at all. If a dress is too short in the bodice so the waist seam sits above the natural waist, there is rarely enough fabric to lengthen it. If the shoulders are far too narrow, the sleeve and armhole would need rebuilding. Recognising these early saves you from accepting a job you will fail.

Pulling lines mean tight, bagging folds mean loose, diagonal lines point to the cause.
Keep wearing ease; remove design ease only when the client chooses a closer style.
Write precise amounts on the job card, not vague instructions.

The fitting is the most important 15 minutes of any alteration job. A good fitting gives you exact marks to sew to. A rushed fitting gives you guesses, and guesses lead to second and third fittings that you cannot charge for. This lesson shows a fitting routine you can repeat with every client, from a single trouser hem to a full gown.
A safety pin
Pins, chalk and a tape measure are the three tools you use most at every fitting.
Before the client arrives

**Kit ready:** fine glass-head or dressmaker's pins in a pincushion, safety pins for heavy fabric, tailor's chalk or a chalk pencil (white and one colour), a tape measure, a hem marker or a metre rule, a full-length mirror and your fitting cards.
**Private space:** a curtained corner or room where she can change. Never ask a client to undress where passers-by or apprentices can see.
**Ask her to bring** the shoes she will wear and the underwear she will wear. A bra with different support or heels of a different height can change a fit by several centimetres.
Respect and consent

Tell the client what you are about to do before you touch her: "I am going to pin at your side seam now." Keep your hands flat on the garment, not the body. If the client is a child, a parent or guardian stays in the room. Clients return to tailors they trust.
The fitting routine
Put the garment on the client **right side out**, fully closed, in her event shoes. Let her stand naturally with weight on both feet, arms relaxed.
**Look before you pin.** Walk around her once. Note drag lines, the hem level and where the seams hang.
Ask her to sit, raise her arms and bend slightly. Some garments look perfect standing and pull badly when she sits.
**Pin from the top down:** shoulders first, then bust, waist, hip, and the hem last. Changes higher up can change the length lower down.
Pin out excess **evenly on both sides** unless her body is clearly uneven. Pin parallel to the seam, pinching the same amount on left and right.
Mark the hem: measure a fixed height from the floor all round, putting a pin every 8 to 10 cm.
Let her look in the mirror and agree. Then remove the garment carefully so the pins stay in.

Working from the top down stops a change at the shoulder from spoiling a hem you already marked.
Marking a level hem

Floors and bodies are not perfectly level, so do not simply fold up the same amount all round. Instead, decide the finished length at the centre front, then measure that height from the floor. Keep the ruler upright and move around the client, marking the same height every 8 to 10 cm while she stands still. You move, she does not.
Worked example: marking and cutting a trouser hem

For example, Tunde brings work trousers that drag on the floor. He wears them with the leather shoes he has on. The current finished inside-leg length is 82 cm and the hem allowance turned up inside is 4 cm.
With his shoes on, you fold the trousers up until the hem just touches the top of the shoe at the front with a slight break. You pin there and measure the new finished inside leg: 76 cm.
Shortening amount = 82 - 76 = 6 cm.
You unpick the old hem. The leg now measures 82 + 4 = 86 cm from crotch seam to raw edge.
You keep a 4 cm hem allowance, so the cut line is 76 + 4 = 80 cm from the crotch seam. You cut off 86 - 80 = 6 cm.
You chalk a line 76 cm from the crotch seam as the new fold, check both legs measure the same, then neaten and hem.
Both legs finish at 76 cm with the same 4 cm hem allowance. Because you kept the allowance the same, the amount cut off equals the amount shortened: 6 cm.

Clients often ask alterers for style advice: "Should I shorten it?", "Will it look better tighter?". Good advice turns a small job into a loyal client. This lesson gives you three simple tools for that advice: **line**, **proportion** and **colour**. You will use them to explain what an alteration will do to the look, so the client chooses with open eyes.
A person posing while being photographed in an outfit
Line, proportion and colour decide how a finished outfit looks in photos and in person.
Line: where the eye travels

The eye follows lines in clothing. **Vertical lines** (front plackets, princess seams, long V-necklines, a single colour from neck to hem) lead the eye up and down, so the outfit looks longer. **Horizontal lines** (a hem, a waist seam, a wide belt, a band of contrast fabric) stop the eye and draw attention to that spot. An alteration moves lines. When you shorten a skirt you move a horizontal line; when you take in a waist you make the waist line more visible.
A hem that ends at the **narrowest part** of the leg (just below the knee, or above the ankle) usually looks lighter than a hem that ends at the widest part of the calf.
A waist seam that sits on the client's **natural waist** looks balanced. A waist seam that sits too low or too high makes the bodice look short or long.
Removing a wide contrast band, or replacing it with a narrow piping, can make a gown look longer without changing its length.
Proportion: dividing the body

Many stylists use a simple guide: outfits divided roughly into one-third and two-thirds look more pleasing than outfits cut exactly in half. A short blouse over a long skirt, or a long top over slim trousers, follows this idea. It is a guide, not a rule, and culture matters: a classic iro and buba has its own balance that clients know and love. Use proportion to explain choices, never to criticise a body.
Talk about the garment, not the body

Many books group bodies into shapes such as pear, apple, hourglass or rectangle. These labels can be useful in your head, but avoid saying them to clients. Instead say what the garment will do: "Ending the hem here shows the slimmest part of the leg", not "Because your calves are big".

Colour: matching thread and trims

In alterations, colour matters most in small choices: thread, zip, lining, piping or a replacement button. On the traditional painter's colour wheel the **complementary** pairs are red and green, yellow and purple, blue and orange. Complements placed side by side look bold and strong. **Analogous** colours, the neighbours on the wheel such as blue, blue-green and green, look calm and harmonious.

Fluorescent tubes and LED bulbs change how colours look. Hold the thread spool against the garment by a window or at the door before you choose. If you cannot find an exact match, a shade slightly darker usually hides better than one lighter.
Worked example: advising on a skirt length

For example, Grace, a teacher in Ibadan, brings a straight ankara skirt that ends 4 cm above her ankle bone. She asks you to shorten it to the knee because she wants it to look "modern". The skirt is a narrow pencil style with a 20 cm back slit.
You measure: knee length would remove about 40 cm, and the 20 cm slit would disappear completely.
You explain that a narrow skirt at knee length needs a walking slit or vent of its own, otherwise she cannot take a full step. A new 12 to 15 cm slit would have to be made.
You offer two options: (a) knee length with a new back slit, or (b) a midi length ending just below the widest part of the calf, keeping about half of the existing slit.
She tries on the skirt pinned at both lengths and looks in the mirror from the side.
Grace chooses the midi length. You record "shorten 18 cm, keep slit, re-finish slit top". Because she saw both options pinned, she is confident, and she does not come back unhappy.
When to say no

Some requests will not give the result the client imagines. A dress that is far too small cannot become comfortable if the seams hold only 1 cm of allowance. A cheap polyester gown may show old needle holes when let out. Satin and some silks mark permanently where stitches are removed. Say so before you start, show her the seam allowance or the fabric, and offer a realistic option. An honest no keeps your reputation; a failed job damages it.
Alterations move lines: hems and waists are horizontal lines the eye stops on.
Use one-third to two-thirds proportions as a guide, never as a judgement on a body.
Match thread one shade darker if you cannot find an exact colour; check in daylight.
Pin options on the client so she sees the result before you cut.

Reading a Garment Before You Alter It

A garment can only be changed as far as its construction allows. This module teaches you to inspect seams, darts and allowances to work out how much a garment can be let out or taken in, then applies that thinking to two areas clients often want changed: necklines and sleeves.
Seam allowances, darts and the letting-out calculation
Inspect a garment and record the usable allowance in each seam
Use the rule that each seam line moved changes the circumference by twice that amount
Calculate whether a garment can be let out enough before accepting the job

Taking in is almost always possible: you can sew a seam deeper as long as the style allows. **Letting out is limited** by how much fabric is hidden inside the seams. Before you accept a letting-out job, turn the garment inside out and do a seam inventory. Ten minutes of measuring saves you from promising a size the garment can never reach.
A straight ruler
A short ruler or seam gauge lets you measure each seam allowance quickly and accurately.
What you are looking for inside

**Seam allowance** is the fabric between the stitching line and the cut edge. Home sewing patterns commonly use 1.5 cm. Ready-made clothes often use 1 cm or less, especially on overlocked seams. Tailored trousers and some gowns are made with wider allowances at the centre back so they can be let out.
**Darts** are stitched folds that shape fabric over the bust, waist or hips. A dart can be let out by sewing it narrower, which gives back some of its intake.
**Seam finish.** An overlocked (serged) seam is usually trimmed narrow, so there is little to let out. Pressed-open seams with neatened edges often have more.
**Hidden extras:** a deep hem, a deep facing, or a wide centre-back seam can all give extra fabric.
Leave a safe seam

You cannot use the whole allowance. After letting out, leave at least about 1 cm of fabric beyond the new stitching on woven fabric, and more on fabric that frays easily such as loosely woven linen or some lace. A seam with only a few millimetres left will pull apart.
The doubling rule

Every seam joins two layers of fabric. When you move the stitching line 1 cm outwards on a seam, **each** of the two panels gains 1 cm, so the circumference grows by 2 cm. A skirt has two side seams, so moving both side seams out by 1 cm adds 4 cm in total. The same rule works for taking in: move both side seams in by 1 cm and the skirt loses 4 cm.

Worked example: can this skirt be let out enough?

For example, Bisi brings a lined ankara pencil skirt she wore before having her baby. Her hip is now 102 cm. The skirt hip measures 101 cm. She wants to sit comfortably at church, so you agree at least 5 cm of hip ease, a target of 107 cm.
Extra needed = 107 - 101 = 6 cm.
Side seams: allowance 2 cm each edge, keep 1 cm safe, so 1 cm usable per edge. Two side seams give 1 x 2 x 2 = 4 cm.
Centre-back seam with zip: allowance 1.5 cm, keep 1 cm, so 0.5 cm usable per edge. One seam gives 0.5 x 2 x 1 = 1 cm.
Total possible = 4 + 1 = 5 cm. New hip = 101 + 5 = 106 cm. Ease = 106 - 102 = 4 cm.
The lining must be let out by the same amounts, so you check its seams too: they have the same allowance.

You can reach 106 cm, not 107 cm. You tell Bisi honestly: the skirt will fit with 4 cm of ease, a little snug when sitting. She can accept that, or you can insert matching side panels from her leftover fabric. You do not promise 107 cm.
Will the old stitching show?

When you move a seam outwards, the old stitching line becomes part of the visible garment. On many cottons and ankara prints the needle holes close after washing and pressing. On some fabrics they never disappear.
**Satin, taffeta, silk and coated fabrics:** needle holes stay visible. Test by unpicking 2 cm at the bottom of a seam and pressing.
**Denim and dark cottons:** the area inside the seam has faded less, so a darker stripe can show along the old line.
**Lace:** let out only within the lining or along a motif edge; lace seams are often overlapped and trimmed.
**Stretch knits:** old stitching can leave a permanent wavy line.
Test before you promise

If you are unsure, unpick a small section inside a hem or at the lower end of a seam, press it with a pressing cloth, and show the client the mark in daylight. Let her decide whether she accepts it before you go further.
Seam ripper safety

Point the seam ripper away from your body and your other hand. Cut stitches every few centimetres rather than pushing the ripper along the seam, which can slice the fabric itself. Keep rippers and scissors closed and out of children's reach.

Reshaping a neckline is an alteration that changes the style, so it must be done carefully. Once you cut, the fabric is gone.

Step by step: lowering a round neckline
**Mark on the client.** With the garment on, place a pin at the new centre-front depth. Ask her to wear the bra she will wear and check that straps and the bra top will be covered.
**Transfer to the garment.** Lay it flat, fold it in half at centre front, and chalk the new curve on one half. Cut both layers together through the fold so both sides match exactly.
Before cutting, **mark a seam allowance**: the chalk line is the finished edge, so cut about 1 cm outside it for the facing seam.
**Staystitch** about 1 cm from the new raw edge, sewing from shoulder towards centre front on each side. This single line of stitching stops the curved bias edge from stretching.
Unpick and remove the old facing. Use it as a guide to cut a new facing that follows the new curve, about 5 to 6 cm deep, with interfacing if the original had it.

Sew the facing right sides together along the neckline, trim and clip the curve every 1 to 1.5 cm, then **understitch**: stitch the facing to the seam allowances close to the seam so the facing rolls inside and does not show.
Press, then tack the facing down at shoulder seams by hand.

Will it go over the head?

A garment without a zip or button opening must pass over the head. Measure around the client's head over her hair or wrap, around the widest point, and measure the neckline edge on the garment. In woven fabric with no stretch, the neckline opening must be at least as big as the head measurement or she cannot get it on. If you are making a neckline smaller, for example by adding a lace insert to raise it, you may need to add a short back opening with a button and loop.
Worked example: a V-neck for an event blouse

For example, Amaka has a plain round-neck silk-look polyester blouse with a back zip. She wants a V-neck to show a gold pendant at her sister's wedding. The pendant hangs 18 cm below the base of her throat.
At the fitting you pin the V point 20 cm below the base of the throat, so the pendant sits 2 cm above the point. You check from the side that the bra is not visible.
On the flat blouse, you chalk straight lines from the V point to where the old curve meets each shoulder seam, so the neck width at the shoulder stays the same and the shoulders still sit correctly.
You staystitch 1 cm inside the chalk lines before cutting, and stitch the V point with short stitches for strength.
You cut a new V-shaped facing 5 cm deep from matching lining fabric with light fusible interfacing.

After sewing the facing, you clip exactly into the V point up to, but not through, the stitching, then turn, understitch as far as you can reach and press with a pressing cloth on a low iron setting suitable for polyester.
The V sits flat, the point is sharp, and the pendant is framed. Because the back zip already gives an opening, you did not need to check head size, but you note it on the card for reference.
Iron temperature

Synthetic fabrics like polyester and nylon can melt or go shiny under a hot iron. Always test the iron on a seam allowance first, use a pressing cloth, and switch the iron off and stand it upright when you walk away. Keep the cord where nobody can trip or pull it down.

Gaping is the other common neckline complaint, especially on V-necks and wrap tops. Small gaping of about 1 cm can often be removed with a tiny dart under the facing at the edge, hidden on the inside. Larger gaping usually comes from the shoulders being too wide or too long, and is better solved by taking in at the shoulder seam, which you will meet in the dress lesson.
Necklines can be lowered or reshaped easily, but raising one needs an added panel.
Cut both sides at once on the fold so the new neckline is symmetrical.
Staystitch the new edge before handling it; understitch the facing so it stays inside.
Check bra coverage and head size before you cut.

Recognise sleeve jobs that need more work than the client expects

Sleeves are a frequent request: too long on a ready-made shirt, too wide on a lace blouse, or simply out of style. Some sleeve jobs are quick. Others, such as shortening a sleeve with a buttoned cuff, take far more time than clients realise. Knowing the difference helps you price and schedule properly.
A coat with long sleeves
Sleeve length is checked with the arm relaxed and bent, not stretched straight out.
Measuring sleeve length correctly

Ask the client to stand with arms relaxed at her sides. For a long sleeve, the finished edge usually sits at the wrist bone or just below it. Then ask her to bend her elbow and reach forward: the sleeve rises, and if it now rides far up the arm it was too short already. For jackets worn over shirts, many tailors leave a little of the shirt cuff showing, often around 1 cm. Pin the new length on both arms, because arms are not always the same length.

Clients notice when a cuff or decorative edge does not look like the original. Unpick slowly, keep every piece of trim in a labelled bag, and photograph the original edge before you start so you can copy the pleats, buttons and stitching exactly.

Most sleeves have one seam, under the arm. That seam has two layers, so the doubling rule applies: moving the stitching in by 1 cm narrows the sleeve by 2 cm all round. Narrowing is usually tapered: more at the upper arm or forearm, and a smooth line into the armhole so the underarm does not become tight.

Worked example: narrowing wide blouse sleeves

For example, Ifeoma has a cotton blouse with wide, straight sleeves that catch on things when she cooks. Her upper arm measures 32 cm. The sleeve measures 44 cm around at the upper arm and 30 cm at the wrist edge. She wants the sleeves slimmer but still comfortable.
Agreed upper-arm width with ease: 37 cm. Reduction = 44 - 37 = 7 cm. Distance to move the stitching = 7 / 2 = 3.5 cm.
Agreed wrist width: 27 cm. Reduction = 30 - 27 = 3 cm. Distance to move the stitching = 3 / 2 = 1.5 cm.

You chalk a new line 3.5 cm inside the old seam at upper-arm level and 1.5 cm inside at the wrist, joining them with a smooth line, and curve back to 0 cm at the underarm point so the armhole stays the same.
You check that her hand passes through: she makes her hand narrow by tucking the thumb in, and her hand measures 21 cm around at that point, well under the 27 cm wrist width.
You tack the new seam first, she tries it on, bends her elbow and lifts her arms, and only then do you sew and neaten it.
The sleeve is 37 cm at the upper arm and 27 cm at the wrist. It no longer catches on pot handles, and she can still move freely.
Do not change the armhole by accident

If you carry a narrowing line into the armhole seam, you make the armhole smaller and the whole sleeve will pull when she lifts her arm. Always curve your new line back to the original seam just below the underarm point.
Restyling a sleeve
**Long to three-quarter or elbow length:** quick if the sleeve has a plain hem. Check the new hem width fits around the forearm or elbow, which is wider than the wrist.
**Removing puffiness at the cap:** reduce the gathers at the top of the sleeve and re-set the sleeve. This takes time and skill and should be priced as a bigger job.
**Removing sleeves completely:** the armhole must then be finished with a facing or bias binding, and may need to be raised slightly at the underarm so the bra does not show.

Always pin and try both sleeves. Bodies are rarely perfectly symmetrical, and a difference of 1 cm in sleeve length between left and right arms is common. Write left and right separately on the job card when they differ.
Check sleeve length with arms relaxed and with the elbow bent.
Cuffed sleeves take much longer to shorten than plain-hemmed ones; price them accordingly.
A single underarm seam means the stitching moves half of the total reduction.
Curve narrowing lines back into the original seam before the armhole.

Core Alterations: Bodices, Waists, Trousers, Skirts and Gowns

This is the heart of the course: the alterations clients ask for every week. You will take in and let out bodices using side seams, darts and the zip seam, reshape trousers and skirts at the waist, seat and leg, and plan a full gown alteration with linings and an event deadline.
Taking in and letting out bodices: side seams, darts and the zip
Share a waist reduction between side seams and darts so the shape stays balanced
Work around a zip in a side seam or centre-back seam
Match a bodice change to the skirt at a waist seam
Tack and test before sewing permanently

Taking in a bodice is the alteration you will do most often on dresses, blouses and gown tops. The beginner's mistake is to take all the extra out at the side seams. That pulls the side seams forward or back, flattens the bust shape and can make darts point to the wrong place. A professional result **shares** the reduction between several seams and darts so the garment keeps its original shape, only smaller.
A fitted dress
Bodice alterations share the change between side seams and darts so the dress keeps its shape.
Where the reduction can come from
Place
How it removes width
Best for
Side seams
Each seam moved 1 cm removes 2 cm
General reduction at waist, bust and hip
Front and back waist darts
Stitching each dart leg 0.5 cm further in adds 1 cm to the dart's intake
Shaping the waist without moving the side seams
Close shaping over the bust and waist on fitted gowns
Centre-back seam
Moved 1 cm removes 2 cm
Back waist hollows, sway back, extra back width
What is dart intake?

The intake is the full width of fabric a dart folds away at its widest point. If a dart is 3 cm wide at the waist and you stitch each leg 0.5 cm further towards the centre, the dart becomes 4 cm wide: 1 cm more is removed. Keep the dart point in the same place, or move it only slightly, so the shaping still aims at the bust or hip.
Working with the zip

Most fitted dresses close with a zip in the centre back or the left side seam. You have three choices. **Take in the other seams only**, leaving the zip alone: quickest, fine for small changes. **Take in the zip seam above and below the zip**, tapering to the zip: rarely neat. **Remove the zip, take in the seam and re-insert the zip**: the correct method when the zip seam must change by more than a few millimetres. An invisible zip must be re-sewn with an invisible zip foot close to the coils.
Choosing where to take in
Small change, no zip seam
Small change, darts plus sides
Zip seam re-set needed
Rebuild or refuse
Amount to remove (small to large)
Need to keep shape (low to high)
The bigger the change and the more shaped the garment, the more seams and darts must share it.
Worked example: taking in a lined dress with a waist seam

For example, Zainab, a nurse in Abuja, has lost weight and wants her lined ankara dress for a staff party in two weeks. The dress has a waist seam, two back waist darts, a side zip on the left and a gathered skirt. Bodice waist: 86 cm. Her waist: 76 cm. She wants about 4 cm of ease, so the target is 80 cm.
Reduction needed at the waist = 86 - 80 = 6 cm.

Right side seam and left zip seam: you move each 1 cm in at the waist, tapering to 0 at the underarm. Two seams x 2 layers x 1 cm = 4 cm. The left zip is removed and re-set because it sits in a seam you are changing.
Two back darts: you increase each dart's intake by 1 cm (0.5 cm further in on each leg). 2 darts x 1 cm = 2 cm.
Total removed = 4 + 2 = 6 cm. New bodice waist = 86 - 6 = 80 cm.
The skirt waist edge must also become 80 cm so the waist seam matches. You unpick the waist seam, pull up the gathers by 6 cm more, and re-join.
The lining is altered by the same amounts, so it does not pull or bag inside.

The bodice and skirt both measure 80 cm at the waist seam, the side seams still hang straight, and the darts still point at the bust. You tack everything first and she approves it at a second fitting before you sew.
Letting out a bodice

Letting out follows the same logic in reverse, limited by the seam inventory from Module 2. Darts can be sewn narrower, which gives back part of their intake. Side seams can be let out only as far as the allowance allows. If a bodice is tight across the bust only, letting out the side seams near the bust and the side bust darts slightly is often enough. If it is tight everywhere, check whether the dress has enough allowance before you accept the job.
Pin or chalk the new stitching lines on the inside with the garment inside out, using the fitting card numbers.
Tack (long hand stitches or the longest machine stitch) along the new lines.
Fit again. Look for side seams swinging, darts pointing wrongly, and pulling at the zip.
Sew the final seams with a normal stitch length, then unpick the old stitching and tacking.
Trim excess seam allowance only on a take-in, never below about 1.5 cm, so the garment can be let out again later.
Neaten the seam edges and press seams open or to the back as the original was.
Leave room for the future

Clients' bodies change with pregnancy, illness, age and seasons. When you take in, do not trim seam allowances to almost nothing. Leaving 1.5 to 2 cm lets you or another tailor let the garment out again later, and clients appreciate it when you tell them.
Machine safety

Keep fingers at least a finger's width away from the needle, never sew over pins (pull them out just before the needle reaches them), and switch the machine off at the wall before changing the needle, the foot or oiling it. Unplug the iron and machine when you leave the room.
Share a reduction between side seams and darts to keep the original shape.
Increasing each dart leg by 0.5 cm adds 1 cm to the dart's intake.
If the bodice changes at a waist seam, the skirt must change by the same amount.
Tack and fit before sewing, and leave 1.5 to 2 cm of allowance for future letting out.

Trousers and skirts: waistbands, seat seams, tapering and original hems
Take in or let out trousers at the centre-back seam through the waistband
Taper a trouser leg evenly using the inseam and outseam
Shorten jeans while keeping the original hem
Adjust a skirt waistband without spoiling its shape

Trousers and skirts bring in steady weekly work: school trousers, office trousers, jeans, and skirts that need a smaller waist. These garments have a waistband, a zip fly or side zip, and often pockets, so you must plan where to make the change without disturbing these parts.
A pair of blue jeans
Jeans and trousers are the most frequent alteration jobs: waists, tapering and hems.
Trouser waist: the centre-back route

Many men's and some women's tailored trousers are made with a **split waistband** joined at the centre back and a **wide centre-back seam allowance**, often 2 to 4 cm, specifically so they can be altered. This is the easiest route for waist and seat changes because you do not touch the zip fly or the pockets.
Unpick the belt loop at the centre back, then the waistband lining and the waistband seam for about 8 to 10 cm on each side of the centre back.
Chalk the new centre-back line. To take in 4 cm in total, move the line 2 cm in at the waist, tapering smoothly to the original seam in the seat curve, about two-thirds of the way down the seat.
Sew the new seam continuously through the waistband and down the seat seam, so the waistband and trousers stay in one line.
Press the seam open, re-close the waistband lining by hand or machine, and re-attach the belt loop.
Try on: check that the back does not pull under the seat when she sits.
Jeans are different

Most jeans have a one-piece waistband and a flat-felled seat seam with two rows of topstitching. Taking in jeans at the back usually means removing the waistband centre section and re-topstitching to match, which takes much longer. Price and schedule jeans waist jobs as a bigger task.
Tapering a trouser leg

A trouser leg has two seams: the inseam (inside leg) and the outseam (outside leg). To keep the crease and the leg hanging straight, take the reduction **equally from both seams**. With two seams and two layers each, move each seam by one quarter of the total reduction at that point.
Pin leg on client
Measure knee and hem
Divide reduction by four
Chalk both seams equally
Blend into thigh
Splitting the change equally between inseam and outseam keeps the crease centred.
Worked example: tapering wide office trousers

For example, Chika wants her wide-leg office trousers slimmer. The leg measures 50 cm around at the knee and 46 cm at the hem. She wants 46 cm at the knee and 38 cm at the hem, and the thigh unchanged.
Knee reduction = 50 - 46 = 4 cm. Each seam moves 4 / 4 = 1 cm.
Hem reduction = 46 - 38 = 8 cm. Each seam moves 8 / 4 = 2 cm.
Check: 2 seams x 2 layers x 2 cm = 8 cm at the hem, and 2 seams x 2 layers x 1 cm = 4 cm at the knee.
You chalk the new lines 2 cm in at the hem and 1 cm in at the knee on both seams, then blend smoothly back to the original seams at mid-thigh.
You check that her foot passes through: her heel-to-instep measurement is 31 cm, well under the 38 cm hem, so she can still put the trousers on easily.
Both legs measure 46 cm at the knee and 38 cm at the hem, the crease stays centred, and both legs are cut identically by folding them together to trim.
Shortening jeans and keeping the original hem

Clients often want jeans shortened but love the faded, factory-stitched hem. The **original hem method** keeps it. You fold the leg up to make a tuck that removes the length, sew close to the old hem, then fold the hem back down.
Mark the new length on the client in her usual shoes. Suppose she wants 5 cm shorter.
Turn the leg right side out and fold the hem up by half the amount: 5 / 2 = 2.5 cm. A fold of 2.5 cm uses up 5 cm of length because it has two layers.
Pin evenly all round, measuring 2.5 cm from the top edge of the original hem band to the fold.
Using a zipper foot and denim thread or a strong polyester thread matched to the denim, sew all round just below the bottom edge of the original hem band.
Trim the excess inside to about 1 cm, neaten with overlock or zigzag, then fold the original hem down and press. Topstitch close to the seam on the leg if you want the tuck to stay flat.
Skirt waists and waistbands

For a skirt with a waistband, take in at the side seams or darts below the band, then shorten the waistband by the same total amount and re-attach it. On a skirt with a facing instead of a band, take in the facing seams at the same places as the skirt seams so the facing lies flat. For elastic waists, it is usually faster to open the casing at a seam, shorten the elastic and re-close it.
Change the band, not just the skirt

If you take 4 cm out of the skirt but leave the waistband the same length, the skirt will be eased or gathered into the band and look puckered. The band must be shortened by exactly the amount you took from the skirt top edge.
Tailored trousers are designed to be altered at the centre-back seam and split waistband.
Taper legs equally on inseam and outseam: each seam moves a quarter of the total.
For an original-hem shortening, fold up half the amount you want to remove.
Shorten a skirt waistband by the same amount you remove from the skirt.

Find an old pair of jeans or denim scraps with a factory hem.

Gown and occasion-wear alterations: order of work, linings and deadlines
Assess a gown fully and list every alteration in the correct order
Raise shoulders and adjust the bodice without spoiling the armhole
Shorten a lined or lace-edged gown hem correctly
Plan fittings and sewing time backwards from the event date

Wedding guests, bridesmaids and aso-ebi groups bring gowns that must be perfect on one fixed date. Gowns carry linings, lace, beads and sometimes boning, and they are expensive. This is high-value alteration work, but it also carries the most risk. A clear assessment, the right order of work and a written plan keep you and the client safe.
A calendar pad
Occasion-wear alterations are planned backwards from the event date.
Assess everything first
Construction: lining or not, boning in the bodice, type of zip, where the seams and darts are.
Decoration: lace motifs, beads, sequins or stones near any seam you will change.
Fabric: does it mark when unpicked? Does it fray? Is it stretch?
Fit on the client in her event shoes and underwear, with every problem listed on the fitting card.
Existing damage such as a broken zip pull, missing beads or stains, written down and shown to the client before you accept the gown.
Record damage at intake

Photograph any stain, pull, missing bead or broken part in front of the client when you receive the gown, and note it on the job card. Without this record, a client may believe the damage happened in your workshop.
Order of work
Gown alteration order
Shoulders and straps
Bust and bodice
Waist and hips
Zip re-set
Hem and lining last
Each step can change the length below it, so the hem is always finished last.

**Shoulders first.** If a gown is too long in the bodice, the bust shaping sits too low and the waist drops. Taking up the shoulder seams lifts the whole bodice. A 1.5 cm shoulder take-up lifts the bust shaping and the waistline by about 1.5 cm. It also raises the underarm and makes the armhole smaller, so check that the armhole does not cut into her arm afterwards. On a gown with sleeves, the sleeve may need to be unpicked and re-set.

**Bodice and waist next**, sharing the reduction between seams and darts as in lesson 3.1. On boned bodices, the boning channels sit on the seams. You must remove the boning from any channel you change, alter the seam, then re-insert boning cut to the new length with its ends tipped or covered so they do not poke through.
Hems on gowns
**Lined gowns:** shorten the outer gown and the lining separately. The lining is usually finished a little shorter than the gown, commonly about 2.5 cm, so it never peeps out below the hem.
**Lace hems with a scalloped edge:** do not cut the scallop off. Remove the lace border, shorten the gown from the top of the border area, then re-apply the border by hand along its motifs.
**Beaded hems:** remove beads in the seam path and save them in a labelled container. Sew them back on after stitching.
**Full or circular skirts:** let them hang for a day before marking the hem, because bias areas drop.
Worked example: planning an aso-ebi gown alteration

For example, Kemi brings a lined lace aso-ebi gown on a Monday for a wedding on Saturday in 12 days. It needs shoulders raised 1.5 cm, the bodice taken in 4 cm, and the hem shortened 8 cm, with a scalloped lace border. You estimate the work time for each task.
Shoulders and re-setting the armhole edge: 45 minutes. Bodice take-in on side seams and darts, outer and lining: 90 minutes. Zip removal and re-set: 40 minutes.
Hem: remove the lace border 40 minutes, shorten the gown and lining 40 minutes, re-apply the border by hand 120 minutes.
Pressing and final check: 25 minutes.
Total = 45 + 90 + 40 + 40 + 40 + 120 + 25 = 400 minutes, which is 6 hours 40 minutes of work.

You plan: fitting 1 today; shoulders and bodice tacked by Thursday; fitting 2 on Friday; hem marked at fitting 2 and finished by the following Wednesday; final fitting and collection on Thursday, two days before the wedding.

Kemi has a written plan with two fittings and a collection two days before the event, which leaves time for any last small fix. You enter 6 hours 40 minutes of work in your weekly schedule so you do not accept too many other jobs.

Aim to finish occasion wear at least two days before the event. If anything goes wrong, from a power cut to a client's change of shoes, you still have time to fix it without panic.
Pressing lace and beads

Assess and photograph the gown, including existing damage, before accepting it.
Work from shoulders to hem; the hem and lining are always last.
Lining is finished a little shorter than the gown so it never shows.
Plan backwards from the event and finish at least two days early.

Restyling: Giving Old Garments a New Life

Restyling goes beyond fitting: you change the style of a garment the client already owns. This module teaches you to judge whether a garment is worth remaking, to calculate whether there is enough fabric, and to carry out two complete restyle projects using alteration skills from earlier modules.
Remake or not? Assessing a garment and checking fabric yield
Assess an old garment's fabric, seams and condition before agreeing a restyle
Measure usable fabric areas and check that new pattern pieces fit inside them
Explain grain and why pieces must be cut on the same grain as the original
Agree a written restyle brief with a sketch and an honest risk note

Clients bring sentimental and valuable garments for restyling: a mother's lace iro and buba, a wedding guest gown worn once, a husband's old kaftan, a wrapper that is still beautiful but no longer fashionable. Restyling reuses good fabric and gives the client something new without buying new cloth. It also takes longer than a normal alteration, and the fabric is limited to what is already there. Assessment is everything.
A person making an eco-friendly choice
Restyling reuses good fabric that would otherwise sit unused in a wardrobe.
The assessment checklist
Is it worth remaking?
Fabric strong, not thin
No fading at folds
Enough usable area
Client loves the fabric
Time fits the budget
If any of these fails, discuss it with the client before agreeing the job.
**Fabric strength.** Hold the fabric up to light and pull gently on the bias. Thin, weak or rotting fabric, especially around underarms and collars, will tear when re-sewn.

**Fading and marks.** Old garments fade unevenly. The inside of seams, the area under a collar and the inside of hems are often darker than the rest. Plan pieces so that faded and unfaded areas do not sit side by side.
**Stains and holes.** Mark them with chalk on the outside so you cut around them.
**Construction.** Is the garment glued, fused or heavily embroidered? Embroidered areas cannot be cut through without spoiling the design.
Grain matters

The **lengthwise grain** runs parallel to the selvedge and is the strongest, most stable direction. In an existing garment, the grain usually runs from shoulder to hem. When you cut a new piece, place its grainline parallel to the old garment's lengthwise grain. A piece cut off-grain will twist and hang badly, even if it is the right size.
Taking the garment apart
Photograph the garment front and back before you start.
Unpick seams rather than cutting along them; you gain the seam allowances as usable fabric.
Press each piece flat with steam (if the fabric allows) to remove creases and old stitching lines.
Label each piece with chalk on the wrong side: front, back, sleeve, and an arrow showing the lengthwise grain.
Measure each piece's usable rectangle, avoiding stains, holes and faded lines, and write it down.
Worked example: will an old kaftan make an A-line skirt?

For example, Ngozi brings her late father's cotton kaftan and wants an A-line skirt from it to keep his memory close. After unpicking and pressing, the front and back body panels each give a clean rectangle 70 cm wide and 100 cm long, with the grain running down the length. Each sleeve gives 50 cm by 55 cm.
Her hip is 100 cm. Your skirt pattern has a front and a back piece, each 58 cm wide at the widest point (hem) and 65 cm long, including seam and hem allowances.
Front piece: 58 cm fits within 70 cm width, and 65 cm fits within 100 cm length, with the grain matching. It fits.
Back piece: the same check on the back panel. It fits. Leftover strip on each panel: 70 - 58 = 12 cm wide and 100 - 65 = 35 cm long below the piece.
The skirt needs a waist facing. The front facing is 36 cm long and the back facing 36 cm, each 6 cm deep. Both fit across a sleeve rectangle 50 cm wide.
You chalk a small embroidered motif from the kaftan's neckline as a patch for the skirt pocket, so a recognisable part of his garment shows.

This lesson brings together everything from Modules 1 to 3 in two complete projects. Each one is popular with clients and makes good portfolio pieces. Read both, then choose one to complete as your practice task.
A shirt
An oversized shirt can be reshaped into a fitted blouse with side seams, darts and shorter sleeves.
Project 1: an oversized shirt into a fitted blouse

A large men's cotton shirt in a good print or a crisp plain colour can become a fitted women's blouse. The work is mainly taking in, with back darts added for shape, and shortening the sleeves. The important limit is the **shoulders**: a men's shirt shoulder will sit beyond her shoulder bone. You either accept a soft, dropped-shoulder look, which suits casual styles, or remove the sleeves, narrow the shoulders and re-set the sleeves, which is advanced work and must be priced as such.
Worked example: shaping the shirt

For example, Aisha wants her brother's old shirt as a fitted blouse to wear with jeans. Shirt chest: 120 cm, shirt waist: 118 cm. Her bust: 96 cm, waist: 82 cm. She chooses a dropped-shoulder casual look, 8 cm of bust ease and 10 cm of waist ease.
Target bust = 96 + 8 = 104 cm. Reduction = 120 - 104 = 16 cm. Side seams: 16 / 4 = 4 cm moved in on each side seam at bust level.
Target waist = 82 + 10 = 92 cm. Reduction = 118 - 92 = 26 cm.
Side seams at the waist: moved in 5 cm each, removing 5 x 2 x 2 = 20 cm.
Two new back waist darts, each with 3 cm intake: 2 x 3 = 6 cm. Total = 20 + 6 = 26 cm.
The sleeves are taken in along the underarm seam in a continuous line with the side seam, then shortened to elbow length with a new hem.

The blouse measures 104 cm at the bust and 92 cm at the waist, with soft dropped shoulders. Because the side seam and sleeve seam are sewn in one continuous line from hem to sleeve end, you can do both in one pass on most shirts.
Unpick the shirt hem at the side seams for about 5 cm so you can re-hem neatly afterwards.
Turn inside out, chalk the new side seam and sleeve line in one continuous curve, tack and fit.
Sew the darts and seams, trim and neaten (most shirts use flat-felled seams; a neat overlock or French seam is fine for the new seam).
Shorten the sleeves and re-hem, then re-close the shirt hem at the sides.
Press and photograph before and after for your portfolio, with the client's permission.

Alterations are many small jobs with short deadlines, so they need their own system. This module shows you how to take in, tag and schedule garments so nothing is lost or late, and how to price each alteration from the time it really takes and its difficulty.

An alteration business may have 20 or 30 garments in the workshop at once, many of them looking alike: five pairs of black trousers, three aso-ebi gowns in the same lace. One mixed-up garment can lose a client and cost you the price of the item. A simple counter system prevents this and lets you promise dates you can keep.
A tag label
A numbered tag on every garment is the simplest way to stop mix-ups.
Intake: five things for every garment
**Tag it.** Pin or tie a numbered tag to the garment (for example 0127). Write the same number on the job slip and in your job book or phone note.
**Write the job slip.** Client name and phone number, garment description, every alteration with exact amounts from the fitting card, price agreed, deposit paid, and collection date.
**Photograph the garment** front and back, and close-ups of any existing stains, pulls, missing buttons or beads. Show the client and note them on the slip.
**Empty the pockets** in front of the client and hand back anything you find.
**Give the client her copy** of the slip, or a WhatsApp photo of it, and keep yours.
Group similar jobs

Hang garments by job type: all hems together, all waist jobs together, gowns separately. Doing all the trouser hems in one session saves time because you change thread and machine settings less often.

How much work can you accept?

Time your jobs for two or three weeks, from picking up the garment to hanging it finished. Write the minutes on each job slip. You will soon know your real times. Then compare the total minutes of work booked for the week with the minutes you actually have for sewing, after fittings, cooking, children, church and travel to the market for supplies.
Worked example: can she take one more gown this week?

For example, Rukayat runs alterations from a room in her house in Ilorin. Booked: hems 10 x 30 = 300 minutes; waists 4 x 75 = 300 minutes; zips 2 x 45 = 90 minutes; gown 240 minutes.
Total booked = 300 + 300 + 90 + 240 = 930 minutes, or 15 hours 30 minutes.
She is already 30 minutes over her 900-minute planning limit before any new job.
Rukayat does not promise another gown this week. She offers the new client a date next week, or a rush slot only if she moves her own rest day, at a rush price.

Many alterers price by guessing or by copying the shop next door. That leads to cheap prices on slow, difficult jobs and arguments when a gown takes four times as long as a hem. A time-based method is fair to you and easy to explain to clients: the price follows the work.
A stopwatch
Timing your jobs is the foundation of fair alteration prices.
Step 1: your hourly rate

Start with what you want to earn in a month, then add your monthly running costs: thread, needles, chalk, zips you keep in stock, electricity or fuel for a generator, phone data and transport to the market. Divide by the hours you can actually sell. Do not count every hour you are in the workshop: fittings, buying supplies, cleaning and messages also take time, so billable hours are fewer than working hours.
Worked example: setting an hourly rate

For example, Esther in Port Harcourt wants to take home about 150,000 naira a month. Her running costs are about 30,000 naira a month. She works 20 days a month and can bill about 5 hours a day. All naira figures here are illustrations only; use your own numbers.
Monthly total needed = 150,000 + 30,000 = 180,000 naira.
Billable hours = 20 days x 5 hours = 100 hours.
Hourly rate = 180,000 / 100 = 1,800 naira an hour, which is 30 naira a minute.
Esther's working rate is 1,800 naira an hour. Every price on her list starts from this number.
Step 2: price each job

**Price = (minutes x rate per minute x difficulty factor) + materials**, then round to a tidy figure. The **difficulty factor** covers risk and skill: delicate fabric, beads, linings, boning, or a garment that is costly to replace. Use 1.0 for simple jobs on easy fabric, and higher factors, such as 1.25 or 1.5, for risky ones. Materials are anything you supply, like a new zip, elastic or interfacing.

Step 3: price list, deposits and explaining prices
**Publish starting prices** ("from 1,000 naira") on a WhatsApp Business catalogue or a printed card, and confirm the final price after the fitting.
**Deposits:** take a deposit on gowns, restyles and any job where you buy materials, for example half the price. Small hems can be paid at collection.
**Explain with time:** "This gown hem takes about four hours because the lace border is sewn back by hand." Clients accept a price more easily when they understand the work.
**Review prices** every few months: re-time your jobs and recheck your costs, especially when fuel, electricity or thread prices change.
Do not discount by guessing

If a client asks for a lower price, offer a lower-cost option rather than the same work for less, for example a machine blind hem instead of a hand-finished one, or a longer turnaround instead of rush.
Keep a simple record

Write every job, its minutes, price and payment method in one notebook or spreadsheet. At the end of each month, add up income and costs. If your real hours per job are higher than your price list assumes, raise the price or speed up your method.

Finally, decide your **re-fix rule** and write it on the price card. For example: small adjustments to your own work are free within seven days of collection if the client brings the garment back with her slip. Changes she asks for later, or a new style, are a new job at the normal price. A clear rule protects your time and makes clients trust you, because they know you stand behind your work.

Ease
The room between body and cloth
Ease = garment measurement minus body
Wearing ease: room to breathe, sit, move
Design ease: extra room for a style
Ask how she will wear the garment
Ease is the difference between the body and the garment at the same place. If her bust is 96 cm and the blouse measures 104 cm, the blouse has 8 cm of ease.
Wearing ease is the minimum room to breathe, sit and move. A common guide for a fitted woven garment is about 2.5 cm at the waist.
Design ease is extra room added on purpose, like in a kaftan. Take it all out and it pulls at the hips when she sits.
So always ask how she will wear it.
Drag lines
The garment shows you the problem
Fine wrinkles stretched across the body, like rays. The area is too tight.
Soft, deep folds that hang. There is too much room there.
Lines at an angle point to the part that needs more or less length or width.
A drag line is a fold or wrinkle, and its direction points to the cause. Horizontal pulling lines across the hips of a skirt mean the hip is too tight.
Vertical folds at the back waist of a dress mean too much width there.
Diagonal lines point to the part that needs more or less length or width. Look first, then measure, then decide. Never pin before you understand the cause.

Remember
Ease = garment minus body at the same place
Pulling means tight, bagging means loose
Fit in her shoes; pin top down, hem last
Mark hems at a fixed height from the floor
Record numbers and places she confirms
To remember. Ease is garment minus body. Pulling means tight, bagging means loose. Fit in her event shoes and pin top down. Mark hems from the floor. Write numbers she confirms.

Reading a garment: seam allowances, necklines and sleeves.
This is the video for module 2 of Fashion Basics and Clothing Alterations.
Why this matters
A garment can only change so far
Check the seams before you accept a job
Use the doubling rule
Reshape a neckline cleanly
Narrow a sleeve without making it tight
Taking in is almost always possible. Letting out is limited by how much fabric is hidden inside the seams. Ten minutes of measuring saves you from promising a size the garment can never reach.
You will learn the doubling rule, and use it on necklines and sleeves.
Seam inventory
Turn it inside out and look
Seam allowance: stitching to cut edge
Darts can be sewn narrower
Overlocked seams are usually trimmed narrow
A deep hem or wide centre back gives extra
Seam allowance is the fabric between the stitching and the cut edge. Home patterns often use 1.5 cm. Ready-made clothes often use 1 cm or less.
A dart can be let out by sewing it narrower.
An overlocked seam is usually trimmed narrow, so there is little to let out.
A deep hem, a deep facing or a wide centre-back seam can give you extra fabric. Write down the allowance at every seam.
Can Bisi's skirt be let out?
Leave at least about 1 cm of seam allowance after letting out.
Move a seam 1 cm: circumference grows 2 cm
Two side seams, 1 cm usable: 4 cm
Centre back, 0.5 cm usable: 1 cm
Total 5 cm: hip 106, not 107
Every seam joins two layers. Move the stitching 1 cm outwards, and each panel gains 1 cm, so the circumference grows by 2 cm.
You cannot use the whole allowance. Leave about 1 cm beyond the new stitching, and more on fabric that frays, or the seam will pull apart.
For example, Bisi's skirt hip is 101 cm and she needs 107. Each side seam has 2 cm, so 1 cm is usable on each edge. Two side seams give 4 cm.
The centre back has 1.5 cm, so 0.5 cm is usable. That gives 1 cm more.
Total 5 cm. The hip can reach 106, not 107. You tell her honestly that it will be a little snug when sitting, or offer side panels from her leftover fabric. You do not promise 107.
Old stitching
Will the old line show?
Often fades
Many cottons
Ankara prints
After washing and pressing
May stay visible
Satin, taffeta, silk
Denim: a darker stripe
Stretch knits: a wavy line
When you let a seam out, the old stitching line becomes visible. On many cottons and ankara prints, the needle holes close after washing and pressing.
On satin, silk and coated fabrics they stay. So unpick 2 cm at the bottom of a seam, press it, and show her the mark in daylight. Let her decide before you go further.
Necklines
Lowering a round neckline
Mark the new depth on the client
Fold at centre front, cut both sides at once
Cut 1 cm outside the chalk line
Staystitch 1 cm from the new edge
New facing, clip the curve, understitch
Press and tack at the shoulders
A neckline can be lowered or reshaped, but raising one needs an added panel, because once you cut, the fabric is gone. Mark the new depth with her bra on, and check the straps are covered.
Fold the garment at centre front and cut both layers together, so both sides match. Cut about 1 cm outside your chalk line for the seam.
Staystitch 1 cm from the new edge, from shoulder to centre front. This one line stops the curved edge stretching.
Cut a new facing, clip the curve every 1 to 1.5 cm, and understitch so the facing rolls inside. A garment with no opening must still go over her head, so measure first.
Sleeves
Narrowing wide sleeves
Upper arm: 44 minus 37 = 7 cm, move 3.5
Wrist: 30 minus 27 = 3 cm, move 1.5
Curve back to 0 at the underarm
Tack, try on, then sew

For example, Ifeoma's wide blouse sleeves catch on things when she cooks. One underarm seam has two layers, so you move the stitching half the reduction. At the upper arm, 7 cm less means moving 3.5 cm.
At the wrist, 3 cm less means moving 1.5 cm.
Curve the line back to the original seam below the underarm. If you carry it into the armhole, the sleeve pulls when she lifts her arm.
Check her hand passes through, tack the seam, and let her bend her elbow and lift her arms before you sew. Remember, a cuffed sleeve takes much longer to shorten, so price it accordingly.
Work safely
Ripper, iron and cords
Point it away from you. Cut every few centimetres, never push it along the seam.
Polyester can melt. Test on a seam allowance, use a pressing cloth.
Switch off and stand it upright when you walk away. Keep the cord out of the way.
Point the seam ripper away from your body and your other hand. Pushing it along a seam can slice the fabric. Keep rippers and scissors closed and away from children.
Polyester and nylon can melt or go shiny under a hot iron. Test on a seam allowance and use a pressing cloth.
Switch the iron off and stand it upright when you walk away, and keep the cord where nobody can trip or pull it down.
Key points
Remember
Do a seam inventory before letting out
Move a seam 1 cm: circumference changes 2 cm
Keep about 1 cm safe allowance
Staystitch and understitch new necklines
Curve sleeve lines back before the armhole

To remember. Check the seams before you accept a letting-out job. Moving a seam 1 cm changes the circumference by 2. Keep about 1 cm safe. Staystitch and understitch a new neckline. And curve sleeve lines back before the armhole.

This is the video for module 3 of Fashion Basics and Clothing Alterations.
Why this matters
The jobs clients bring every week
Take in a bodice and keep its shape
Taper trousers and keep the crease
Shorten jeans with the original hem
Plan a gown back from the event date
This is the heart of the course: the alterations clients bring every week.
You will also keep the factory hem on jeans, and plan a gown so it is ready in time.
Taking in a bodice
Share the reduction
Beginner's mistake
All of it from the side seams
Side seams swing
Darts point the wrong way
Professional result
Side seams and darts share it
Seams hang straight
Original shape, only smaller
The beginner's mistake is to take it all out at the side seams. That pulls them forward or back, and makes darts point the wrong way.
A professional shares the reduction between seams and darts, so the garment keeps its original shape, only smaller. Stitch each dart leg 0.5 cm further in, and the dart removes 1 cm more.
Worked example
Zainab's lined dress: remove 6 cm
Tack and fit before you sew. Leave 1.5 to 2 cm of allowance.
Waist 86 cm, target 80: remove 6 cm
Two seams in 1 cm each: 4 cm
Two back darts 1 cm more each: 2 cm
Skirt and lining change by the same 6 cm
For example, Zainab, a nurse in Abuja, has lost weight. Her bodice waist is 86 cm, and with about 4 cm of ease the target is 80. So 6 cm must come out.
Move the right side seam and the left zip seam in 1 cm each, tapering to nothing at the underarm. That removes 4 cm. The zip sits in a seam you are changing, so it is removed and re-set.
Make each of the two back darts take 1 cm more. That is 2 cm. Total, 6 cm.
The skirt waist must also become 80 cm, so the waist seam matches, and the lining is altered the same way so it does not pull.
Tack first, and fit again before you sew. Never trim the allowance below about 1.5 cm, so the dress can be let out again later.
At the machine and iron
Fingers a finger's width from the needle
Never sew over pins
Switch off at the wall to change needle or foot
Unplug machine and iron when you leave

Keep your fingers at least a finger's width from the needle, and pull pins out just before the needle reaches them. Switch off at the wall before changing the needle or the foot, and unplug the machine and iron when you leave the room.
Trousers
Inseam and outseam share it equally
Each seam moves a quarter of the reduction
Knee 50 to 46: move each seam 1 cm
Hem 46 to 38: move each seam 2 cm
Tailored trousers are made to be altered at the centre-back seam. To slim a leg, take equally from the inside and outside seams, to keep the crease centred.
Two seams with two layers each means each seam moves a quarter of the total.

For example, Chika's leg is 50 cm at the knee and 46 at the hem. She wants 46 and 38. So each seam moves 1 cm at the knee and 2 cm at the hem, blending back at mid-thigh. Check her foot still passes through.
Jeans
Keep the original hem
Mark the new length in her usual shoes
Fold up half the amount: 5 cm needs 2.5
Sew just below the original hem band
Trim to 1 cm, neaten, fold down, press
Clients love the faded factory hem on their jeans. Suppose she wants them 5 cm shorter.
Fold the hem up by half the amount, 2.5 cm. The fold has two layers, so it uses up 5 cm of length.
With a zipper foot and strong thread matched to the denim, sew all round just below the original hem band.
Trim the inside to about 1 cm, neaten it, fold the hem down and press. Compare both legs.
Gowns
Order of work: top to hem
Photograph any damage before you accept
Shoulders first, then bust and bodice
Waist and hips, then the zip
Hem and lining last, lining a little shorter
Gowns are high value and high risk. Photograph any stain, pull or missing bead in front of the client, and write it on the job card.
Work from the top. Taking up the shoulders 1.5 cm lifts the bust shaping and waist by about 1.5 cm. Check the armhole does not cut into her arm.
The hem is always last, because every change above can change the length. Finish the lining about 2.5 cm shorter so it never peeps out, and never cut off a scalloped lace border.
Plan the deadline
Kemi's aso-ebi gown in 12 days
Finish occasion wear at least two days before the event.
Estimate each task in minutes
Total: 400 minutes, 6 hours 40
Two fittings in the plan
Collection two days before the wedding
For example, Kemi's lace gown needs shoulders raised, the bodice taken in and the hem shortened, with a scalloped border re-applied by hand.
Adding every task gives 400 minutes, which is 6 hours 40 minutes. Put that in your weekly schedule so you do not accept too many other jobs.
Plan backwards from the event, with two fittings, and collection two days before the wedding. If there is a power cut or she changes her shoes, you still have time.
Key points
Remember
Share a reduction between seams and darts
Change the skirt by the same amount
Each trouser seam moves a quarter
Original hem: fold up half the amount
Gowns: shoulders first, hem last, finish early

To remember. Share a reduction between seams and darts, and change the skirt to match. Each trouser seam moves a quarter. For an original hem, fold up half. On gowns, shoulders first, hem last, and finish early.

Restyling: is it worth remaking, and is there enough fabric?
This is the video for module 4 of Fashion Basics and Clothing Alterations.
Why this matters
Good fabric, a new life
Judge whether a garment is worth remaking
Check the fabric is big enough
Agree a written brief before you cut
Two popular restyle projects
Clients bring precious garments: a mother's lace iro and buba, a gown worn once, a husband's old kaftan. Restyling gives them something new without buying new cloth.
But the fabric is limited to what is already there, and the work takes longer than a normal alteration. So assessment is everything.
Before you agree

Hold the fabric to the light and pull gently on the bias. Thin or weak fabric, especially at underarms and collars, will tear when re-sewn. Look for uneven fading at folds and seams, and chalk around stains and holes.
If any check fails, discuss it with the client before you agree the job.
Taking it apart
Unpick, press, label, measure
Photograph it front and back
Unpick seams, do not cut along them
Press each piece flat
Label each piece with a grain arrow
Measure each usable rectangle
Photograph the garment before you start.
Unpick the seams rather than cutting. You gain the seam allowances as usable fabric.
Press each piece flat, if the fabric allows steam.
Label each piece on the wrong side with an arrow for the lengthwise grain. It usually runs from shoulder to hem. A piece cut off grain will twist and hang badly, even if it is the right size.
Then measure each clean rectangle, avoiding stains, holes and faded lines.
Fabric yield
Will a kaftan make an A-line skirt?
Body panels: 70 by 100 cm each
Skirt piece: 58 wide, 65 long. It fits.
Facings fit across a sleeve, 50 cm wide
Neckline embroidery becomes a pocket patch
For example, Ngozi brings her late father's cotton kaftan and wants an A-line skirt. After unpicking and pressing, each body panel gives a clean 70 by 100 cm, with the grain running down the length.
Each skirt piece is 58 cm wide and 65 cm long. 58 fits in 70, and 65 fits in 100, with the grain matching. It fits.
The waist facings are 36 cm long, so they fit across a sleeve piece.
And a small embroidered motif from his neckline becomes the pocket patch, so a part of his garment still shows.
Agree it before you cut
A restyle cannot be undone. Get her yes in writing.
A simple sketch, even in biro
What will be kept, what will change
Risks, said honestly
Fittings and collection date
Draw a simple sketch, and write what will be kept and what will change.
Write the risks. For Ngozi: old fabric, so the seams will be reinforced, and slight fading near old seams. If she is grieving, take extra care to explain what will be cut.
Add the fittings and collection date, and send a photo of the brief on WhatsApp. Keep her reply saying yes, go ahead.
Project 1
An oversized shirt into a fitted blouse
Bust 120 to 104: move each side seam 4 cm
Waist 118 to 92: remove 26 cm
Side seams 5 cm each: 20 cm
Two back darts of 3 cm: 6 cm
For example, Aisha wants her brother's shirt as a fitted blouse. With 8 cm of ease, her bust target is 104 cm, so 16 cm comes out. Divided by four, each side seam moves 4 cm.
Her waist target is 92 cm, so 26 cm must come out.
Moving the side seams 5 cm each removes 20 cm. Two new back darts of 3 cm remove 6 more. Total, 26.
Sew the side seam and sleeve seam in one continuous line, then shorten the sleeves to the elbow.
Be honest
The shirt's shoulders
Dropped shoulder
Accept the wide shoulder
A soft, casual look
Quick to do
Re-set sleeves
Remove and narrow shoulders
Advanced work
Price it as a bigger job
A men's shirt shoulder will sit beyond her shoulder bone. She can accept a soft, dropped-shoulder look, which suits casual styles. Aisha chose this.
Or you remove the sleeves, narrow the shoulders and re-set the sleeves. That is advanced work, so tell her and price it that way.
Project 2
A maxi dress gains sleeves
Cut line: 120 plus 3 cm hem = 123 cm
Strip below: 22 cm tall, 180 cm around
Two sleeves: 46 + 46 = 92 cm wide
88 cm left for a head wrap or belt
For example, Funke's sleeveless maxi is 145 cm long. She wants 120 cm with cap sleeves for church. Add a 3 cm hem, and the cut line is 123 cm from the shoulder.
That leaves a strip 22 cm tall and 180 cm around. Each sleeve is 14 cm tall, so it fits, cut on the same grain as the dress.
Two sleeves need 92 cm of width. The sleeve is 2 cm wider than her 44 cm armhole, and that small extra is eased in at the shoulder.
88 cm is left for a matching head wrap or belt. But pin a paper sleeve on the dress, and get her approval, before you cut the hem.
Key points
Remember
Check strength, fading and marks first
Unpick, press, label the grain, measure
Every piece must fit, grain the same way
Agree a written brief and sketch
Pin a paper pattern before you cut

Every new piece must fit with the grain the same way. Agree a written brief, and pin a paper pattern before you cut.

Running an alteration service: tags, minutes and fair prices.
This is the video for module 5 of Fashion Basics and Clothing Alterations.
Why this matters
Many small jobs need a system
Never lose or mix up a garment
Promise only dates you can keep
Price from the time a job really takes
You may have 20 or 30 garments in the workshop at once. Five pairs of black trousers, three gowns in the same lace. One mix-up can lose a client and cost you the price of the item.
So you need a simple counter system, a way to know how much work you can accept, and prices that follow the work.
Intake
Five things for every garment
Tag it with a number, for example 0127
Write the job slip with exact amounts
Photograph it, including existing damage
Empty the pockets in front of her
Give her a copy of the slip
Pin a numbered tag to the garment, and write the same number on the job slip and in your job book.
The slip carries her name and phone, every alteration with exact amounts, the price, the deposit and the collection date.
Photograph the garment, with close-ups of any stains, pulls or missing buttons, and show her.
Empty the pockets in front of her, and give her a copy of the slip, or a WhatsApp photo of it.
Capacity
Can she take one more gown?
5 hours a day, 6 days: 30 hours
Half kept free: 900 minutes to plan
Already 30 minutes over: no new gown
Time your jobs for two or three weeks, and write the minutes on each slip. For example, Rukayat in Ilorin can sew about 5 hours a day, 6 days a week. That is 30 hours.
She keeps half free for fittings, buying supplies and jobs that take longer than planned. That leaves 900 minutes.
She has booked 10 trouser hems, 4 waist take-ins, 2 zips and a gown. That is 930 minutes.
She is already 30 minutes over, so she offers the new client a date next week, or a rush slot at a rush price.
Your hourly rate
What Esther needs each month
For example, Esther in Port Harcourt bills about 5 hours a day, 20 days a month.
Take-home income target
Running costs a month
Naira figures are illustrations only.
Many alterers price by guessing, or copy the shop next door. That leads to cheap prices on slow, difficult jobs. Start instead with an hourly rate.
Esther wants to take home about 150,000 naira a month.
Her thread, needles, zips, fuel, data and transport cost about 30,000.
So she needs 180,000. Only count hours you can sell. 20 days of 5 hours is 100 hours. 180,000 divided by 100 is 1,800 naira an hour, or 30 naira a minute.
Pricing by time
Minutes, rate, difficulty, materials
Trouser hem, 30 minutes: 1,000
Jeans, original hem, 45 minutes: 1,500
Waist take-in, 75 minutes: 2,500
Lace gown hem, 240 minutes, 1.5: 11,000
Price equals minutes, times your rate per minute, times a difficulty factor, plus materials. Then round it. A plain trouser hem of 30 minutes, at 30 naira a minute, is 900, rounded to 1,000 naira.
Jeans with the original hem take 45 minutes, so 1,500. A waist take-in of 75 minutes, 2,500.
A lined lace gown hem takes 240 minutes, with a difficulty factor of 1.5 for the risk. That is about 11,000 naira. It looks like just a hem, but it takes eight times as long.
Worked example
Pricing a zip replacement
For example, Esther replaces a broken invisible zip on a cotton skirt in 50 minutes.
Time: 50 minutes at 30 a minute
New invisible zip
The fabric is ordinary cotton, so the difficulty factor is 1.0.
50 minutes at 30 naira a minute is 1,500.
She supplies the new zip, about 500 naira.
The price is 2,000 naira. If the client wants it the same day and Esther must move another job, she adds a rush charge of 50 percent of the labour, 750 naira, making 2,750.
Collection
Handing over, safely
Confirm payment in your own app, never from a screenshot.
She tries it on, or you check the measure
Reminders when ready, and after a week
Uncollected rule agreed in writing
Measurements and photos kept private
At collection, let her try on fitted work, and fix small issues on the spot if you can.
Send a polite reminder when it is ready, and again after a week. Write your rule for uncollected items on the slip at intake, so she agrees to it.
Keep your job book out of sight, and never post her garment or measurements without asking.
Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are common. Check the money has arrived in your own bank or wallet app before you hand anything over.
Key points
Remember
Tag, slip, photograph, empty pockets, copy
Plan in minutes, keep spare time
Rate = (income + costs) ÷ billable hours
Charge for rush work, take deposits
Confirm payment before release

To remember. Tag, slip and photograph every garment. Plan in minutes and keep spare time. Build your rate from income and costs over billable hours. Charge for rush work, take deposits on gowns and restyles, and confirm payment before you release.
